title: Design exercise: metrics and time series pipeline
summary: A classic design exercise: a metrics system for tens of millions of series with dashboards, alerts and tiered retention. The reference answer sizes the sample stream from stated assumptions and the Gorilla compression figure, decouples ingestion from storage with a samples log, keeps a compressed 26-hour window in memory, compacts into immutable blocks with downsampled tiers, narrows queries through an inverted index, and treats cardinality as the unit of capacity with hard per-tenant limits.

exercise.prompt: Design the metrics system for a company's services: thousands of instances emit counters, gauges and histograms every few seconds, engineers query the last few hours on dashboards and alerts, and a few people need a year of history at coarser resolution. The system must not fall over when one team adds a label that explodes into millions of series.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Ingest metrics by scrape and by push; store them with labels; answer range and instant queries over labels with aggregation functions; evaluate alerting rules; enforce per-tenant series limits.
Raw data for 15 days; minute aggregates for 90 days; hour aggregates for 15 months.
20,000 service instances, each exposing 2,000 series, so 40 million active series; a 15 s scrape interval.
chosen for the exercise; derive the sample rate, the raw and compressed volumes and the hot-window memory yourself
50 tenants (teams); 500 dashboard and rule queries per second at peak, most over the last hour.
A sample is queryable within 30 s of being scraped; a last-hour query answers in under 1 s at p99 and a 30-day query in under 10 s.
99.9 percent availability for ingestion and for alert evaluation; no single tenant can degrade another's ingestion.
Logs and traces (separate systems that share label conventions), anomaly detection, billing, the dashboard product itself.

clarifying_questions.a: A metric name plus a unique set of label key-value pairs; every distinct combination is a separate stream of (timestamp, value) samples, which is the Prometheus data model.
Pull by default (the scraper controls the rate and knows when a target is down); push for batch jobs and for edge locations that cannot be scraped, through a gateway that applies the same limits.

A label must never carry an unbounded value (user ids, request ids, full URLs); the Prometheus instrumentation guidance says to keep a metric's label cardinality small, below about 10 as its rule of thumb, because every label set is a separate series, and the ingest layer enforces a per-tenant series limit with rejection and an alert when it is hit.

clarifying_questions.q: How exact must old data be?
clarifying_questions.a: Downsampled: for data older than 15 days, 1-minute aggregates (min, max, sum, count) are enough; older than 90 days, 1-hour.
Yes, as bucket series; a histogram with 20 buckets is 22 series, and the sizing counts them.

clarifying_questions.q: Can a query span all tenants?
clarifying_questions.a: No; queries are tenant-scoped, with a platform tenant that may read everything for fleet-level views.

500 queries times a few hundred series each over one hour, 240 samples per series; a memory-bound scan, not a disk one

rows: 320 GB per day times 26 hours, the window Gorilla kept in memory because most queries were for recent data, plus a series header of about 100 bytes per series (assumption), about 4 GB
two replicas of the window: a few dozen large nodes, or more small ones
320 GB per day times 15, in object storage
four values (min, max, sum, count) a minute instead of one every 15 s is about the same bytes per series per day as raw; 320 GB times 90 (assumption: no further compression counted)
instead of 172,800 raw samples; the reason the tiers exist

blocks.text: The hot tier is sized by series, not by samples: the per-series header and the open chunk are what fill memory, and a query that touches millions of series is what times out. That is why the ingest layer enforces a series limit per tenant and why the capacity unit of the platform is a series.

Scrapers pull targets on a schedule (the Prometheus model) and a push gateway accepts what cannot be scraped; both go through an ingest layer that validates labels and enforces per-tenant series limits before anything is stored. Samples land on a partitioned log keyed by series hash, which decouples ingestion from storage and lets the hot store be rebuilt. The hot store keeps the last 26 hours in memory, compressed, replicated twice; a compactor writes 2-hour blocks to object storage and downsamples into tiers. A query frontend splits a query by time range, caches results, and fans out to hot shards and long-term blocks.

blocks.legend: Boxes are containers; the three frames are ingestion, storage and the query path; cylinders are stores; double brackets are logs. Ingestion and storage are decoupled by the samples log: a hot store node can restart and replay without losing a scrape.

blocks.text: Three published systems have this shape. Gorilla at Facebook is a write-through in-memory cache of the most recent 26 hours in front of a durable store, compressing samples to 1.37 bytes on average. Monarch at Google has a regionalised architecture, keeps the data in memory, and pushes query evaluation down as close to the source data as possible. Uber's M3 puts a coordinator in front of the storage nodes that handles downsampling, retention and rollup rules per subset of metrics.

blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed; the open arrow at step 9 is the hand-off: the scraper's acknowledgement does not wait for storage. The registry is consulted only for series the ingest task has not seen in its own cache, so most samples never touch it. Sources: the conditional put s25; the partition key and sequence numbers s8; per-shard write quotas and the aggregation of many samples into one record s9, s10; the interface endpoint s11; Service Connect s18.

blocks.text: The stream has provisioned shards because the load is flat: 43 MB per second around the clock needs about 43 shards at 1 MB per second each, and the design runs 60 for headroom and hot partitions.

Each shard also accepts at most 1,000 records a second, so the ingest task aggregates many samples into one record per shard, the way the Kinesis Producer Library does; without aggregation the record limit, not the byte limit, would be the ceiling.
Part b: the hot store consumes its shards and the compactor writes the blocks, with the two failures that matter: a lost hot task and a compactor that falls behind.

blocks.text: Nothing in the read path writes to the stream or to S3; the only writes are the cache fills. A query that would touch more series than its tenant's limit is refused before any shard is called, which is the read-side half of the cardinality rule.

blocks.caption: The samples log: Kinesis provisioned, Kinesis on-demand, Amazon MSK, or SQS.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, provisioned shards
rows.pick_when: the throughput is known and flat, consumers need per-key ordering and replay, and the producer can aggregate records
rows.avoid_when: the load swings by an order of magnitude within a day, so sized shards sit idle or throttle
rows.example: For this design: chosen. Scraping is flat at 43 MB per second around the clock, so sixty shards at a fixed hourly rate are the cheap shape, each hot task owns a set of shards, and a replacement task replays from its checkpoint.

rows.pick_when: the throughput is unknown or bursty and nobody wants to count shards; it scales from a few MB per second to many GB per second in this Region
rows.avoid_when: a flat, high volume billed per GB written and read costs many times the equivalent shards
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. About 111 TB a month written and read once would cost about eighteen times the provisioned shards for the same bytes.

rows.pick_when: the team already runs Kafka clients, wants its ecosystem and compression, or needs retention and partition counts beyond what a managed stream offers
rows.avoid_when: a small team with no Kafka estate, where brokers to size, patch and rebalance buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: the honest alternative. Three small brokers cost about the same as the shards, and Kafka clients compress batches natively; it would be the pick if the scrapers already spoke Kafka or the log needed days of retention at this volume.

rows.pick_when: one consumer, idempotent work, no ordering and no replay, and the simplest hand-off
rows.avoid_when: consumers need order per key, replay from a position, or several readers of the same data
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The hot store replays its shards from a checkpoint and needs samples per series in order; a queue has neither a position nor an order.

blocks.caption: The hot store and the services: ECS on Fargate, ECS on EC2, EKS, or Lambda.

rows.pick_when: steady, container-shaped services, including stateful ones whose memory fits the largest task size and whose state can be rebuilt from a log
rows.avoid_when: a shard needs more memory than one task offers, local NVMe, or a particular instance family
rows.example: For this design: chosen for everything. The hot store's shard replicas fit the largest Fargate task, 16 vCPU and 120 GB, with eight of them holding the 700 GB window; the scrapers, ingest, compactor, frontend and evaluator are plain stateless tasks scaled on lag and request rate.

rows.pick_when: the memory per shard exceeds the task maximum, or the hot store wants local NVMe for spill and faster restarts, or reserved instances make a steady fleet cheaper
rows.avoid_when: the team wants no instances to patch and the task sizes suffice
rows.example: For this design: the alternative at 10x. Seven terabytes of hot window on tasks of 120 GB is sixty replicas; a memory-optimised instance family with a reservation would hold the same window on fewer, larger nodes.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes, wants its operators for stateful sets, or portability across clouds
rows.avoid_when: a handful of services and no Kubernetes estate; the cluster fee, the upgrade cadence and the SRE time buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen, though a stateful set is the shape many open-source metrics stores ship as; the ECS service scheduler and the log replay give the same recovery without the cluster to run.

rows.pick_when: event-shaped, short, stateless work with spiky volume, paid per request
rows.avoid_when: long-lived state in memory, held connections, or a flat high volume where per-request billing dwarfs the compute
rows.example: For this design: not chosen anywhere on the hot path; a hot store is the opposite of stateless, and the scrapers run continuously.

blocks.caption: The long-term store, the index, and the buy option: S3 and DynamoDB, Timestream, or the managed Prometheus service.

rows.option: Amazon S3 for the blocks, Amazon DynamoDB for the registry
rows.pick_when: the long-term data is immutable blocks read by range, and the index is key lookups at a modest write rate
rows.avoid_when: the long-term queries need a query engine over the raw points rather than block reads
rows.example: For this design: chosen. Blocks are written once and read by time range, the cheapest shape object storage serves; the registry maps a series to its shard and counts series per tenant with conditional writes, which is a key-value workload.

rows.pick_when: the team wants a managed time series database with a memory store and a magnetic store, SQL over the points, and no compactor to run
rows.avoid_when: the data model is Prometheus series and PromQL, and the hot path is an in-memory window the team controls
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Its memory and magnetic tiers mirror this design's hot window and blocks, but the query language and the series model differ from what the dashboards and rules speak.

rows.pick_when: the team wants the Prometheus data model and PromQL without running ingestion, storage or querying, and its volume sits in the cheaper tiers
rows.avoid_when: the volume is tens of millions of series, where the per-sample price tiers add up to far more than the equivalent fleet
rows.example: For this design: the buy option, priced honestly. About 6.9 trillion samples a month would cost about $116,000 in ingestion alone, roughly twelve times this design's bill; it buys the operations this design pays an SRE team for, and is the right call at a tenth of the volume.

rows.option: A relational or wide-column store for the points
rows.pick_when: the points must be joined with other data in SQL at query time
rows.avoid_when: the workload is append-only samples read by series and time range
rows.example: For this design: does not apply; the decision guide's time series and object storage categories cover every store here.

blocks.caption: The results cache: ElastiCache for Valkey, in-task memory, ElastiCache Serverless, or DAX.

rows.pick_when: the cache is shared by all frontend tasks, the working set is small and steady, and a replica covers a node loss
rows.avoid_when: the working set swings widely or is tiny enough to live in each task
rows.example: For this design: chosen, one small node with a replica. Dashboards repeat the same queries every refresh, so a shared cache of sub-range results turns most of the 500 queries a second into cache hits; a lost primary fails over to the replica.

rows.pick_when: each frontend task can hold the working set and a miss is cheap
rows.avoid_when: many tasks each miss the same query, so the shards do the work many times over
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Six frontend tasks would each warm the same buckets; the shared cache does it once.

rows.pick_when: the working set is unpredictable and nobody wants to size nodes
rows.avoid_when: a small, steady working set where one node and a replica cost less than the per-GB-hour charge
rows.example: For this design: not chosen; the working set is a few gigabytes held all day.

rows.pick_when: the cache fronts a DynamoDB table and the reads are item lookups
rows.avoid_when: the cached values are query results, not table items
rows.example: For this design: does not apply; the cached objects are evaluated sub-ranges, not registry items.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: One scrape cycle, one compaction, and one dashboard query; the step numbers run on across the three parts.
Part a: a scrape and its ingestion, with the limit that protects the other tenants.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant T as Target
  participant SC as Scraper
  participant IN as Ingest
  participant IX as Series index
  participant LOG as Samples log
  SC->>T: GET /metrics, per-target timeout
  T-->>SC: exposition text
  opt scrape fails
    Note over SC: an up=0 sample, so absence is visible
  end
  SC->>IN: a parsed batch, tenant attached
  IN->>IX: look up or create each series
  alt the tenant is over its series limit
    IX-->>IN: refused
    IN-->>SC: counted error, not a silent drop
  else within the limit
    IX-->>IN: series ids
    IN-)LOG: append by series hash
  end
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed; the open arrow is the hand-off to the log. Every 15 s each scraper shard scrapes the targets it owns by consistent hashing of the target address s1; the cardinality rule the limit enforces is Prometheus's own guidance s5, s6.

blocks.text: Part b: the hot store consumes the log and the compactor turns closed chunks into blocks and tiers.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 10
  participant LOG as Samples log
  participant HOT as Hot store
  participant CP as Compactor
  participant LT as Long-term blocks
  LOG-)HOT: samples, by partition
  HOT->>HOT: append to the open chunk, compressed
  HOT->>LOG: acknowledge the offset
  Note over HOT: new series update the shard's index
  HOT-)CP: closed chunks, every 2 hours
  CP->>LT: an immutable block with its index
  CP->>LT: the 1-minute and 1-hour aggregates
  LT-->>CP: durable
  CP->>HOT: the block is durable
  Note over HOT: drops data older than 26 hours only now
blocks.legend: Compression is delta-of-delta on timestamps and XOR on values, the Gorilla scheme s2; the hot store never drops data before the block that holds it is durable. The 2-hour block and the tiers follow the M3 shape of retention and rollup rules s4.

blocks.text: Part c: a last-hour dashboard query, and the rule evaluator that uses the same path.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 19 participant Q as Dashboard participant QF as Query frontend participant IX as Series index participant HOT as Hot shards participant LT as Long-term blocks Q->>QF: query_range, last hour QF->>QF: split by tier, check the results cache QF->>IX: which series, which shards IX-->>QF: a small set par to each shard that holds a match QF->>HOT: evaluate the expression locally HOT-->>QF: partial results end opt the range crosses into the tiers QF->>LT: the older sub-range, 1-minute tier LT-->>QF: downsampled points end QF-->>Q: merged result, cached by bucket Note over Q,QF: rules run on this path on a schedule,
replicated and deduplicated
blocks.legend: Pushing evaluation down to the shards that hold the series is Monarch's main argument s3; the rule evaluator is replicated so that an evaluator failure does not silence alerts, and the four golden signals are what most of those rules watch s7.

blocks.text: The bottleneck is cardinality, not bytes. One service that adds a user id label turns 2,000 series into millions overnight; memory per series, not per sample, is what fills the hot tier, and a query that touches millions of series is what times out. The ingest limit per tenant is the control: a hard cap on active series with rejection, a soft cap that alerts, and per-metric cardinality reports so the owning team can see which label did it.

The Prometheus instrumentation guidance (keep a metric's label cardinality below 10; every label set is another series with its own cost) is the rule the limit enforces, and the naming guidance names the values that must never be labels: user ids, email addresses, any unbounded set. Series churn (short-lived pods creating new series on every deploy) is the second-order problem; it is bounded by the same limit and by expiring series that have not received a sample for a window.

blocks.title: Why the tiers exist: one 30-day query
items: A 30-day dashboard panel asks for one series over 30 days.
At raw resolution that is 172,800 samples per series (one every 15 s).
At the 1-minute tier it is 43,200 points, a quarter of the raw count, and the panel cannot show more anyway.
The frontend splits the range at the 15-day boundary and reads the older part from the 1-minute blocks.
A fleet-level query over every tenant never runs ad hoc at full resolution: the platform tenant reads pre-aggregated recording rules.

blocks.text: Reads scale by narrowing before scanning: the inverted index turns a label selector into a small set of series and the shards that hold them, the frontend splits long ranges into cached sub-ranges, and pushing aggregation down to the shards keeps the data where it is, which is Monarch's main argument.
Each row names the failure, what engineers see, and the mitigation.

long-range queries fail; recent queries fine
query frontend returns partial results with a flag; compactor retries; the 26-hour window covers the common case
its targets show up=0 and gaps

the scraper knows when a target is down and controls the rate; push for what cannot be scraped

a year of raw data is about 120 TB compressed (320 GB per day) for nothing most queries need

blocks.text: The cost per million series per month is the number the platform publishes, and the hot tier's memory is most of it, so the levers are the compression ratio (which the Gorilla scheme fixes) and the series limits, which decide how many series exist at all.

L1: Scrape and push ingestion, a time series store with labels, a query API and tiered retention.
The sample rate (2.7 million per second) and raw volume derived from the stated assumptions, with the compressed figure cited.
A per-tenant series limit enforced at ingest, with the cardinality rule stated.
L2: The in-memory hot window with compression, a samples log between ingestion and storage, and 2-hour immutable blocks with an inverted index.
Downsampling tiers and query splitting with a results cache; fan-out to the shards narrowed by the index with pushdown of aggregation.
Replicated rule evaluation and the up=0 convention so absence is visible.
Series churn and the memory-per-series argument as the capacity model.
L3: A multi-tenant metrics platform: regional zones with federation, tenant isolation of partitions, quotas and showback per series and per query.
Cost per million series per month as the number the platform is held to, and recording rules as a necessity at fleet scale.
What the system refuses: unbounded labels, cross-tenant ad hoc queries, dropping hot data before blocks are durable.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: what a series is, pull versus push, the cardinality rule, downsampling, histograms, tenant scoping. Say the numbers aloud: 40 million series, 2.7 million samples per second, 43 MB per second raw and about 3.7 MB per second compressed, a 26-hour hot window of about 700 GB with two replicas.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Series, Sample in compressed chunks, Block with an inverted index, Tenant limits, Rule; the query and series endpoints and the push write endpoint.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: scrapers and push gateway, ingest with limits, the samples log, the hot store, compactor and tiers in object storage, the query frontend. Say what the log buys.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: cardinality as the capacity unit (limits, reports, churn, memory per series), then the query path (index narrowing, splitting and caching, downsampled tiers, pushdown, replicated rules).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x platform (zones and federation, isolation, showback), and the L3 sentence: the unit of capacity is a series, not a byte, and the design is about who may create one.

Context and scope: The services and their instrumentation today, the dashboards and alerts that depend on it, the outage or cost that motivates a new system, and the label conventions shared with logs and traces.
Goals and non-goals: Freshness within 30 s, last-hour queries under 1 s, tiered retention, tenant isolation; logs, traces, anomaly detection and the dashboard product out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: ingestion with limits, the samples log, the hot tier, compaction and tiers, the query frontend and rules.
Alternatives considered: Push everywhere, a disk-based store for everything, direct writes without a log, raw retention forever, best-effort cardinality, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security (tenant scoping on every query, who may change limits), observability of the observability system (ingest lag, rejected samples per tenant, compaction backlog, query p99 by tier, rule evaluation lag), cost per million series per month, rollout by scraping both systems for a tenant and comparing.
Review questions the doc must answer: What happens on the day a tenant doubles its series in an hour, and what a dashboard shows while object storage is unavailable.
